title: A third for food
hookLine: one hadith names the worst vessel to fill, then divides it into three

cards: Cups, bags, inboxes, calendars. A person fills a lot of containers in a day. One hadith singles out one vessel as the worst a human being can fill, and it's carried everywhere, all day, right under the ribs.
Then the hadith does the math. It divides the vessel into three and gives each part a job, including one part whose job is to stay empty. Today's title is the first of the three.

teach.b: The hadith is in Jami' al-Tirmidhi, from al-Miqdam ibn Ma'dikarib. In paraphrase, the Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, said: no human being fills a vessel worse than his stomach.
A few mouthfuls are enough to keep his back upright. And if he must eat more, then a third for his food, a third for his drink, and a third for his breath. Look at the order.
A few mouthfuls first. The thirds are the allowance: if he must. And the last third is kept empty, for breathing.

teach.h: EAT AND DRINK, BUT BE NOT PRODIGAL.
teach.b: The Qur'an puts the principle in one line, in al-A'raf, in Pickthall's translation: "eat and drink, but be not prodigal." Both are commanded; the body isn't the enemy. But not wasteful, not past need.
This isn't the fast of Ramadan, which has its own days and rules. It's a measure for an ordinary lunch, and not a punishment: nothing in the hadith says hunger is holy.
Its picture is a person with a straight back, strong enough to work and to pray.

teach.h: FOOD FOR TWO IS ENOUGH FOR THREE.
teach.b: One more hadith, in Sahih al-Bukhari, shows where the empty third can go: food for two is enough for three, and food for three is enough for four. Room is a courtesy too: to the body, and to whoever eats what you didn't.

how: Muslims cite the hadith of the three thirds when they speak of moderation in eating, alongside the Qur'an's "eat and drink, but be not prodigal," and the saying that food for two is enough for three.

games.q: what does “a third for food” mean?
o: a rule to give a third of your food to charity
the hadith's measure: food, drink, and room to breathe
a fast that skips one meal out of every three

games.q: a third for food — tap the pairs.
p: enough to keep the back upright

s: the hadith says everyone must eat exactly a third
it says a few mouthfuls are enough; the thirds are for whoever must eat more.
one third is left for breath
a third for food, a third for drink, a third for breath.
the Qur'an tells believers to hold back from eating and drinking
al-A'raf: eat and drink, but be not prodigal.

games.q: the plate is half done. you're not hungry anymore, but it's delicious. by the hadith's measure, what now?
o: finish it, so nothing is wasted.
stop, leave room for breath, and save the rest.
eat faster, before you notice you're full.
games.why: the hadith keeps a third empty for breath, and another hadith says food for two is enough for three: what you leave can feed someone else.

practice: Rest one hand lightly on your stomach and notice what's there, empty, half, full, heavy, without a verdict, then breathe in slowly and feel how much room the breath itself takes: that's the third the hadith keeps empty.
Choose the sign that will tell you to stop at your next meal: a slower bite, a sip of water, a breath that comes easily.
If food is a hard subject for you, simply stay with the breath; if you pray, you can say alhamdulillah, praise be to Allah, as you set the plate down.

wordCard.voice: A third for food. The hadith's measure: a few mouthfuls if they're enough, and if not, a third for food, a third for drink, a third for breath. Today's word.

orig.note: Arabic: a third, the hadith's measure for food, drink and breath.

carryVoice: Your line: leave room. The last third is for breath. Tomorrow, the adab of guests.
